extracted.intended_audience: general literate public; readers and contributors of a moral/literary periodical (Spectator), and fellow writers/critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and publishing short moral and literary periodical essays and criticisms for a general readership; includes editorial standards for avoiding scandal, aims of criticism, and moral advice on personal conduct (marriage, solitude, charity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of long courtship
rubrics_metrics.description: Those marriages that are preceded by a long courtship generally abound most with love and constancy; the passion should strike root and gather strength before marriage be grafted on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A long course of hopes and expectations fixes the idea in our minds and habituates us to a fondness of the person beloved. Short courtships risk weak attachment and future complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer good qualities over mere beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing of so great importance as the good qualities of one to whom we join ourselves for life; good-nature, evenness of temper, virtue, and good sense are preferable to celebrated beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good-nature and evenness of temper give an easy companion; virtue and good sense, an agreeable friend; love and constancy, a good spouse. Remarkable beauty without these may bring fears and jealousies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be discerning before marriage, forgiving after
rubrics_metrics.description: Before marriage be inquisitive and discerning in the faults of the person beloved; after marriage be dim-sighted and superficial about minor imperfections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discretion prevents dwelling on disagreeable things; good-nature raises compassion and softens imperfections into beauties. Inspect faults carefully before contracting, then practice forbearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of marriage (love vs interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: A marriage of love is pleasant; a marriage of interest is easy; where both meet, the marriage is happy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek a balance of personal affection and prudent provision — both contribute differently but importantly to marital happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not set the heart on transient things (art of growing old)
rubrics_metrics.description: In growing old, propose that no one set his heart upon what is transient; beauty and fashions change and holding fast to transitory delights breeds misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept flux and change; avoid scornful bitterness toward younger generations; cultivate memory of worthy actions rather than repeated old intrigues or vain reminiscence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pursuing showy appearance over real interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The world is more intent on trains and equipages and the showy parts of life than on true interest; people often labour to appear easy and happy to others rather than to be so in reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise genuine domestic felicity and virtuous conduct over dazzling the multitude; appearances often mislead about real happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial policy: avoid news and party politics
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper contains not a single word of news, a reflection in politics, nor a stroke of party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid partisan content to draw minds off the bitterness of party and furnish subjects of discourse treatable without warmth or passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial policy: avoid immoral, obscene, or defamatory content
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject all things that savour of party, loose and immoral subjects, obscene ideas, satyrs upon priesthood, marriage, and the like, private scandal, or anything tending to the defamation of particular persons, families, or societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though such subjects might sell papers, they are intentionally excluded to preserve decency and avoid injury to private reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care to avoid harming reputations when drawing characters
rubrics_metrics.description: When drawing any faulty character, consider persons to whom the malice of the world may possibly apply it, and dash particular circumstances so as to prevent ill-natured applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check names and particulars (even syllables and letters) to avoid resemblance to real persons; be tender of reputation and scorn diversion at the expense of private men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid offending high figures and creating public offence
rubrics_metrics.description: Take care not to give offence to those who appear in higher figures of life; avoid subjects that might insult public characters or provoke needless scandal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even potentially ludicrous matters (e.g., a procession of waxwork images) may be forborne out of respect and prudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for moral and intellectual improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose discourses that improve the mind and make the heart better; write reflections and speculations apt to improve readers' minds and manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are hidden seeds of goodness in most readers; writing that cultivates virtue and knowledge will find acceptance and do public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism should discover beauties, not merely expose faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms should be intended rather to discover beauties and excellencies in the writers of one's time than to publish their faults and imperfections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on highlighting merits that others may have overlooked; invite others to publish discoveries too rather than merely lampooning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticise the author, not the person
rubrics_metrics.description: It is acceptable to criticise an author so long as one keeps clear of attacking the person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver judgments as private opinion; keep charity in critique and avoid personal invective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invite candour and collaboration in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have made any better remarks, impart them with candour; if not, use the offered observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish criticism as contribution to a shared enterprise of literary improvement and encourage others to add their discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and regularity in literary criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Undertake regular, systematic criticism (e.g., a weekly critique of Paradise Lost) delivered as private opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular, principled attention to a major work demonstrates seriousness and lets readers follow an orderly commentary rather than random attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not affect solitude merely to seem singular
rubrics_metrics.description: Affectation to love the pleasure of solitude is often a pretence among those unfit for retired life; some affect solitude out of sourness or contradiction rather than genuine vocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True separation from the world comes from surrendering the desire to be known, not from theatrical singularity; follow the genuine bent of one's genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best way to withdraw: give up desire of being known
rubrics_metrics.description: The best way of separating oneself from the world is to give up the desire of being known to it; after keeping innocence and performing duties, spending time one's own way makes life free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modesty and private contentment, not ostentation, constitute a laudable retirement from public life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of secret charity and modest living
rubrics_metrics.description: A man who lives modestly and gives the surplus of his fortune in secret to the needy purchases true merit and daily comfort from conscience and blessings of those he helps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than pomp and a visible retinue, secret beneficence and frugal living procure inner satisfaction and social esteem at death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of affectations (example: feigned closeness or contrived poverty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affectations such as feigning covetousness or contrived poverty (as in the example of Irus) are social tactics that manipulate perception and can produce ambiguous moral outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise such behaviours as strategic performances: they may gain social advantage but also deceive and compromise sincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about imitation and forged correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a risk of others imitating an author's manner so closely as to forge letters or assume his air; one should be aware of, and wary about, such mimicry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain awareness of forgeries and imitations; authenticate correspondence and acknowledge that skilled mimicry can mislead readers.
